prompt: `a := [4]int{1, 2, 3, 4}`, `s := a[:]`, then `s[0] = 100`. What does `fmt.Println(a)` print?
hint: How many sets of four `int`s are there?

choices.text: `[1 2 3 4]`, because `a[:]` made a copy
choices.why: Slicing never copies; `s` points at `a`'s first element.

choices.text: `[100 2 3 4]`, changed through `s`
choices.why: Right. There is one array, and `s` is a view of all of it.

choices.text: Nothing: an array cannot be sliced, so it does not compile
choices.why: Lesson 11 sliced arrays, and `a[:]` ran and printed `[100 2 3 4]`.
An assignment to `s[0]` replaces element 0; it does not insert.

prompt: Why is `hex.EncodeToString(sha256.Sum256(data)[:])` refused by the compiler?
hint: Where would the slice point?

choices.text: `hex.EncodeToString` takes an array, not a slice
choices.why: It takes a `[]byte`; passing it `sum` itself is what the other error refused.

choices.text: The returned array is stored nowhere, so it is unaddressable
choices.why: Right. A slice points into an array that lives somewhere, and a call's result does not yet.

choices.text: `[:]` works on slices only, never on arrays
choices.why: `a[:]` on an array variable compiled and ran in section 02.

choices.text: Slicing would copy 32 bytes, and Go never copies implicitly
choices.why: Slicing copies nothing; the trouble is that there is nothing stored to point at.

prompt: The compiler calls the result of a call, not yet stored in any variable, an ___ value, and refuses to slice it.
hint: The error said `cannot slice … value`.

prompt: `a` is a `[4]int` and `s := a[:]`. What are `len(s)` and `cap(s)`?
hint: The slice reaches exactly as far as the array.

choices.text: 4 and 8, leaving room to append
choices.why: The capacity cannot exceed the array, and this array has four elements.

choices.text: 4 and 4, the size of the array
choices.why: Right: the run printed `4 4`, so the first append has to copy.

choices.text: 0 and 4, an empty view with room for four
choices.why: That would be `a[:0]`. With no numbers the view covers the whole array.

choices.text: 4 and 0
choices.why: A capacity is never less than the length.

prompt: `sum := sha256.Sum256(data)`. Which of these compile? Choose all that apply.
hint: `sum` is a variable holding a `[32]byte`.

choices.text: `hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])`
choices.why: Yes, it printed 64 hexadecimal digits.

choices.text: `hex.EncodeToString(sum[:4])`
choices.why: Yes. Any slice expression on the variable gives a `[]byte`; this one covers the first four bytes.

choices.text: `hex.EncodeToString(sum)`
choices.why: Refused: `cannot use sum (variable of type [32]byte) as []byte value`.

choices.text: `hex.EncodeToString([]byte(sum))`
choices.why: An array does not convert to a slice with `T(x)`; the slice expression is the only way across.

prompt: Which of these copies a slice's first four elements into a new array?
hint: One of them is an array type; one is a pointer type.

choices.why: That is a pointer into the slice's own array; writing through it changed `s`.
Right. After `c[0] = 100`, `s` still started with 1.
That is another slice over the same array, and slicing never copies.
A full slice expression limits the capacity; it is still a view of the same array.

prompt: `s := []int{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6}` and `p := (*[4]int)(s)`. After `p[0] = 100`, what does `s` print?
hint: A pointer conversion copies nothing.

choices.why: Right. `p` points at the first four elements of the array `s` views.
That is what the array conversion `[4]int(s)` leaves; the pointer shares.
That is `*p`. The conversion does not shorten `s`, which keeps all six.

choices.text: Nothing: it panics, as `s` has six elements and not four
choices.why: Longer is fine; only a slice shorter than the array panics.

prompt: What happens when `[4]int(s)` runs with `len(s) == 2`?
hint: The compiler does not know a slice's length.

choices.text: The build fails with a conversion error
choices.why: The length is only known at run time, so the program compiled.

choices.text: The last two elements are zero
choices.why: Go does not pad. Padding would hide a short read, and the conversion refuses instead.

choices.text: A panic: `cannot convert slice with length 2 to array or pointer to array with length 4`
choices.why: Right, and the same message covers the pointer conversion.

choices.text: It returns a `[2]int`
choices.why: The array type is written in the conversion; its length is not negotiable.

prompt: Match each `go` line in `go.mod` to what it lets `[4]int(s)` and `(*[4]int)(s)` do.
hint: The pointer conversion is the older of the two.

prompt: A parser does `id := [16]byte(buf)` for each record, then reads the next record into the same `buf`. Does `id` change?
hint: Which conversion was it?

choices.text: Yes: `id` points into `buf`'s array, so the next record shows through it
choices.why: That is `(*[16]byte)(buf)`. An array type, not a pointer type, means a copy.

choices.text: No: the conversion copied sixteen bytes into `id`
choices.why: Right. `id` is an array, a value of its own, like `c` in section 03.

choices.text: Only if `buf` is longer than sixteen bytes
choices.why: A longer `buf` still gives a copy of the first sixteen; the length decides only whether it panics.

choices.text: It does not compile: a slice needs a pointer conversion
choices.why: Since Go 1.20 a slice converts to an array type directly.

prompt: `raw` has length 3 and capacity 8. What does `[4]byte(raw[:4])` do?
hint: Which check does `raw[:4]` pass, and which does it skip?

choices.text: Panics, since `raw` holds only three bytes
choices.why: That is what `[4]byte(raw)` does. `raw[:4]` stretches the slice to four first, inside the capacity.

choices.text: Converts, taking one byte that lies past `raw`'s length
choices.why: Right. `short[:4]` printed four bytes from a three-byte slice, with no complaint.

choices.text: Fails to compile, because 4 is more than `len(raw)`
choices.why: The compiler knows neither the length nor the capacity of a slice.

choices.text: Panics at `raw[:4]` with `index out of range`
choices.why: A reslice is checked against the capacity, 8 here, and 4 is within it.

prompt: Why may `[32]byte` be a map key when `[]byte` may not?
hint: A map has to compare keys.

choices.text: Arrays take less memory than slices, so they hash faster
choices.why: A `[32]byte` is bigger than a slice header. Size is not the rule; comparability is.

choices.text: Arrays compare with `==`; slices only with `nil`
choices.why: Right. A map needs keys it can compare, and `x == y` on two slices was refused.

choices.text: Only types from the standard library may be keys
choices.why: `string` and `[32]byte` are both built from the language, and the rule is about `==`.

choices.text: A slice key would need `make` first
choices.why: `make` does not make a slice comparable; nothing does.

prompt: In the duplicate finder, why was `d.txt` (`hello` and a newline) not reported as a copy of `a.txt`?
hint: What does the key compare?

choices.text: The map compared the file names it stored as values, and those names differ
choices.why: The key is the checksum; the names are only the values stored under it.

choices.text: `==` on arrays compares only the first elements
choices.why: It compares every element; that is why `c.txt` matched `a.txt` exactly.

choices.text: The extra byte gives a different 32-byte checksum, so a different key
choices.why: Right: three different contents, and `d.txt` was one of them.

choices.text: Its checksum was a slice, and slices are never equal
choices.why: `Sum256` returns a `[32]byte` for every file, and arrays compare.

prompt: Which of these compare the contents of two `[]byte` values `x` and `y`? Choose all that apply.
hint: The operator is refused; two functions are not.

choices.text: `bytes.Equal(x, y)`
choices.why: Yes, it printed `true`.
Refused: `slice can only be compared to nil`.

choices.text: `slices.Equal(x, y)`
choices.why: Yes, for slices of any comparable element type, `byte` included.

choices.text: `len(x) == len(y)`
choices.why: That compares two lengths; `hello` and `world` would pass it.

prompt: Comparing two slices with `==` is refused with: `slice can only be compared to ___`.
hint: The one comparison lesson 12 used on slices.

prompt: You need a set of IPv4 addresses read from packets as `[]byte`. Which map type does the job?
hint: Four bytes, compared by value.

choices.text: `map[[]byte]bool`, keyed by the slice as it arrives
choices.why: A slice cannot be a key at all; lesson 14 shows the refusal.

choices.text: `map[*[4]byte]bool`, so that no key is copied
choices.why: Pointers compare by address, so the same address read twice gives two different keys.

choices.text: `map[[4]byte]bool`, keyed by `[4]byte(raw)`
choices.why: Right. The conversion copies the four bytes into a comparable value.

choices.text: `map[[32]byte]bool`, keyed by `sha256.Sum256(raw)`
choices.why: It works, but hashing four bytes into 32 adds a step the address does not need.

prompt: Bytes for an IPv4 address arrive in `raw []byte` from the network. Put the steps in a safe order.
hint: The conversion panics on a short slice.

prompt: `a := [4]int{1, 2, 3, 4}`, `s := a[:]`, `b := [4]int(s)`, then `b[0] = 9`. Which of `a`, `s` and `b` now start with 9?
hint: One step shares and one step copies.

choices.text: All three
choices.why: That needs both steps to share, and the conversion to an array copies.

choices.text: Only `b`
choices.why: Right. `a` and `s` share one array, and `b` is a copy taken out of it.

choices.text: `s` and `b`, but not `a`
choices.why: `s` is a view of `a`; nothing can change one without the other.

choices.text: `a` and `b`, as `s` is a separate copy
choices.why: Slicing never copies, and `b` is the only separate copy here.
